title: P.T.
subtitle: The same corridor becomes less familiar each time
summary: P.T. is Kojima Productions' PlayStation 4 psychological-horror teaser, released on 12 August 2014. An unknown person walks through a domestic corridor that leads back to its own beginning, with each repetition introducing changes that are difficult to anticipate. The player's actions are limited to moving and looking more closely, making attention itself the main means of progress. A small house becomes threatening through repetition rather than scale. The player learns its shape quickly, then loses confidence in what that knowledge can guarantee when the next loop begins.
body: P.T. is Kojima Productions' PlayStation 4 psychological-horror teaser, released on 12 August 2014. An unknown person walks through a domestic corridor that leads back to its own beginning, with each repetition introducing changes that are difficult to anticipate. The player's actions are limited to moving and looking more closely, making attention itself the main means of progress. A small house becomes threatening through repetition rather than scale. The player learns its shape quickly, then loses confidence in what that knowledge can guarantee when the next loop begins.

The bathroom, corridor and returning staircase supply a compact set of spaces in which sounds and small visual differences become important. Cryptic requirements encourage investigation, while the presence of Lisa makes waiting and turning around feel dangerous. The player has few tools for resolving that uncertainty through force. Instead, progress depends on noticing a change and deciding whether approaching it is necessary. The limited layout gives each detail more weight: a light, doorway or noise can alter the meaning of the whole route because there is so little else competing for attention.

Released under the name 7780s Studio, the teaser eventually revealed Silent Hills, a planned collaboration involving Hideo Kojima and Guillermo del Toro. Ludvig Forssell composed its music. Konami removed P.T. from the PlayStation Store after the larger game's cancellation, making an ordinary reinstall impossible. Its influence continued through other horror games and fan recreations. The release demonstrates how a brief interactive work can become memorable through precise limits, using one repeated domestic space to make the player increasingly uncertain about the next few steps rather than promising a larger world beyond them.
